claim: Theoretical accounts distinguish between motivational ('wanting') and hedonic ('liking') dimensions of rewards.
source: Theoretical accounts distinguish between motivational ('wanting') and hedonic ('liking') dimensions of rewards.
evidence: This is a statement about theoretical frameworks in reward research, supported by established scientific literature.

claim: Previous animal and human research linked wanting and liking to anatomically and neurochemically distinct brain mechanisms.
source: Previous animal and human research linked wanting and liking to anatomically and neurochemically distinct brain mechanisms
evidence: This claim references prior research findings in the field.

claim: Reducing opioid receptor activation with naltrexone selectively reduced wanting of rewards.
source: Reducing opioid receptor activation with naltrexone selectively reduced wanting of rewards
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Naltrexone's effect on wanting was reflected by stronger coupling between dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the striatum under naltrexone compared with placebo.
source: which on a neural level was reflected by stronger coupling between dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the striatum under naltrexone compared with placebo.
evidence: This is a neural finding from the study's fMRI data analysis.

claim: Reducing dopaminergic neurotransmission with amisulpride revealed no robust effects on behavior or neural activity.
source: In contrast, reducing dopaminergic neurotransmission with amisulpride revealed no robust effects on behavior or neural activity.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's experimental data.

claim: Opioid receptors mediate neural connectivity related to specifically motivational, not hedonic, aspects of rewards.
source: Our findings thus provide insights into how opioid receptors mediate neural connectivity related to specifically motivational, not hedonic, aspects of rewards.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: 'Wanting' and 'liking' refer to preconscious, rather than conscious, mental states.
source: whereby 'wanting' and 'liking' refer to preconscious, rather than conscious, mental states (Berridge, 1996; Berridge and Kringelbach, 2015; Berridge et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a theoretical definition supported by citations.

claim: Dysfunctions in wanting and liking of rewards belong to the core symptoms of addiction.
source: Dysfunctions in wanting and liking of rewards belong to the core symptoms to addiction, which can be conceptualized as a wanting-dominated state with deficits in switching to liked non-drug rewards (Berridge and Robinson, 2016; Berridge et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about addiction supported by citations.

claim: Dopaminergic activity is thought to modulate the wanting component of rewards, but not liking.
source: Dopaminergic activity is thought to modulate the wanting component of rewards, but not liking (Berridge and Valenstein, 1991).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citation to animal research.

claim: The opioidergic system has been associated with both wanting and liking.
source: In contrast, the opioidergic system has later been associated with both wanting and liking (Berridge and Kringelbach, 2015).
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citation.

claim: Human studies support the hypothesized link between dopaminergic activation and cue-triggered wanting.
source: Human studies support the hypothesized link between dopaminergic activation and cue-triggered wanting (Hebart and Gläscher, 2015; Soutschek et al., 2020b; Weber et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human studies.

claim: Human studies support the link between dopaminergic activation and the motivation to work for rewards.
source: as well as the motivation to work for rewards (Cawley et al., 2013; Chong et al., 2015; Korb et al., 2020; Skvortsova et al., 2017; Soutschek et al., 2020a; Venugopalan et al., 2011; Westbrook et al., 2020; Zénon et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to human studies.

claim: Two studies suggest that dopamine changes only experimental measures of wanting (motivation to work for rewards), but not self-reported wanting ratings.
source: Noteworthy, two of these studies suggest that dopamine changes only experimental measures of wanting (motivation to work for rewards), but not self-reported wanting ratings (Korb et al., 2020; Venugopalan et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Pharmacological manipulations of the opioid system affected both wanting and liking aspects of rewards in humans.
source: Consistent with animal findings, pharmacological manipulations of the opioid system affected both wanting and liking aspects of rewards in humans (Buchel et al., 2018; Chelnokova et al., 2014; Eikemo et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to human pharmacological studies.

claim: Both dopaminergic and opioidergic neurons project to reward circuits in the striatum as well as to the prefrontal cortex.
source: Both dopaminergic and opioidergic neurons project to reward circuits in the striatum as well as to the prefrontal cortex (Delay-Goyet et al., 1987; Lidow et al., 1991)
evidence: This is an anatomical claim supported by citations.

claim: The ventral striatum appears to encode the currently behaviorally relevant reward dimension and dynamically switch functional connectivity with wanting- and liking-encoding prefrontal regions.
source: In particular, the ventral striatum appears to encode the currently behaviorally relevant reward dimension and dynamically switch functional connectivity with wanting- and liking-encoding prefrontal regions (Weber et al., 2018; such frontostriatal gating constitutes one possibility how dopamine [and by extension opioids] can affect functions involving prefrontal cortex and the striatum; Cools, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to neuroimaging findings.

claim: Wanting and liking are preferentially represented in partially distinct subregions of the striatum.
source: This is also in line with the view that wanting and liking are preferentially represented in partially distinct subregions of the striatum (which are in turn connected to different input and output regions; Peciña, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation.

claim: Processing of wanting and liking appears to be dissociable on both a neurochemical and an anatomical basis.
source: Thus, processing of wanting and liking appears to be dissociable on both a neurochemical and an anatomical basis.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on cited literature.

claim: The study investigated the impact of pharmacologically manipulating dopaminergic and opioidergic systems on the neural processing of wanting and liking information.
source: To test this hypothesis, the current study investigated the impact of pharmacologically manipulating dopaminergic and opioidergic systems on the neural processing of wanting and liking information.
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: The study administered a task that allows distinguishing between wanting and liking dimensions of valued goods.
source: Here, we administered a task that allows distinguishing between wanting and liking dimensions of valued goods
evidence: This describes the experimental task used in the study.

claim: The study assessed how pharmacologically reducing dopaminergic (using the dopamine antagonist amisulpride) or opioidergic neurotransmission (with the opioid antagonist naltrexone) changes frontostriatal connectivity related to parametric wanting and liking judgements.
source: and assessed how pharmacologically reducing dopaminergic (using the dopamine antagonist amisulpride) or opioidergic neurotransmission (with the opioid antagonist naltrexone) changes frontostriatal connectivity related to parametric wanting and liking judgements.
evidence: This describes the study's methodology.

claim: The study hypothesized that reducing opioid receptor activation will reduce both wanting and liking.
source: We hypothesized that, on a behavioral level, reducing opioid receptor activation will reduce both wanting and liking (Buchel et al., 2018; Chelnokova et al., 2014; Eikemo et al., 2016)
evidence: This is a stated hypothesis based on prior research.

claim: The study hypothesized that reduced dopaminergic neurotransmission will selectively affect wanting.
source: whereas reduced dopaminergic neurotransmission will selectively affect wanting (Cawley et al., 2013; Korb et al., 2020; Venugopalan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a stated hypothesis based on prior research.

claim: The study hypothesized that the behavioral effects of the pharmacological manipulations are mirrored by changes in frontostriatal connectivity related to wanting and liking information.
source: We further hypothesized that on a neural level the behavioral effects of the pharmacological manipulations are mirrored by changes in frontostriatal connectivity related to wanting and liking information (Weber et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a stated hypothesis based on prior research.

claim: The study expected that frontostriatal connectivity during wanting judgements is modulated by opioidergic and dopaminergic activation.
source: In particular, we expected that frontostriatal connectivity during wanting judgements is modulated by opioidergic and dopaminergic activation (as these neurotransmitters have been related to the processing of wanting)
evidence: This is a stated expectation based on prior knowledge.

claim: The study expected that frontostriatal connectivity during liking judgements should be reduced after reduction of opioidergic neurotransmission.
source: whereas frontostriatal connectivity during liking judgements should be reduced after reduction of opioidergic neurotransmission.
evidence: This is a stated expectation.

claim: Healthy young volunteers rated how much they wanted or liked everyday items in the MRI scanner.
source: We analyzed the data of healthy young volunteers who rated how much they wanted or liked everyday items in the MRI scanner.
evidence: This describes the study procedure.

claim: Wanting and liking ratings were collected for all items in the MRI scanner twice, once before (pre-test session) and once after (post-test session) participants played a game.
source: We collected wanting and liking ratings for all items in the MRI scanner twice, once before (pre-test session) and once after (post-test session) participants played a game on the computer where they won or lost 50% of the items
evidence: This describes the study procedure.

claim: Participants actually received the won items at the end of the experiment.
source: Participants actually received the won items at the end of the experiment (i.e., after the post-test session).
evidence: This describes the study procedure.

claim: Participants received either naltrexone (N = 37), amisulpride (N = 40), or placebo (N = 39) prior to performing the task in the scanner.
source: To test the impact of pharmacologically manipulating dopaminergic and opioidergic receptor activation on wanting and liking, participants received either naltrexone (N = 37), amisulpride (N = 40), or placebo (N = 39) prior to performing the task in the scanner.
evidence: This describes the study design.

claim: No significant Judgement × Item type interaction was observed in the post-test session.
source: Contrary to our previous study (Weber et al., 2018), we observed no significant Judgement× Item type interaction, β = 0.50, t(111) = 1.61, p = 0.11
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's data analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in wanting ratings between won and lost items.
source: However, separate analyses for wanting and liking ratings revealed no significant difference in wanting ratings between won and lost items, β = 0.29, t(115) = 0.64, p = 0.52
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's data analysis.

claim: Liking was more strongly reduced for lost than for won items.
source: whereas liking was more strongly reduced for lost than for won items, β = 01.84, t(115) = 3.16, p = 0.002
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's data analysis.

claim: The effect of decreased liking of lost versus won items replicates a previous finding.
source: with the latter effect replicating our result of decreased liking of lost versus won items (Weber et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research.

claim: Reducing opioid neurotransmission differentially affected wanting and liking ratings.
source: This analysis provided evidence that reducing opioid neurotransmission differentially affected wanting and liking ratings, Naltrexone × Judgement, β = 7.02, t(125) = 2.36, p = 0.02
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's data analysis.

claim: Amisulpride showed no significant effects on wanting or liking ratings.
source: while we observed no significant effects for amisulpride, β = 3.79, t(126) = 1.30, p = 0.20
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's data analysis.

claim: Wanting ratings were significantly reduced under naltrexone relative to placebo.
source: Judgement type-specific analyses suggested that wanting ratings were significantly reduced under naltrexone (mean = 4.5, standard deviation [sd] = 1.0) relative to placebo (mean = 4.9, sd = 1.0), β = –13.85, t(115) = 2.12, p = 0.04, Cohen's d = 0.47
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's data analysis.

claim: Amisulpride showed no significant effects on wanting ratings relative to placebo.
source: whereas amisulpride (mean = 4.9, sd = 1.0) showed no significant effects on wanting ratings relative to placebo, β = –1.39, t(116) = 0.22, p = 0.83, Cohen's d = 0.05.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's data analysis.

claim: Neither naltrexone nor amisulpride showed significant effects on liking relative to placebo.
source: Neither naltrexone (mean = 5.2, sd = 0.9) nor amisulpride (mean = 5.4, sd = 0.8) showed significant effects on liking relative to placebo (mean = 5.2, sd = 0.8), for both t < 1.17, p > 0.24, Cohen's d < 0.27.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's data analysis.

claim: The findings provide evidence for involvement of opioidergic neurotransmission in wanting judgements.
source: Taken together, our findings provide evidence for involvement of opioidergic neurotransmission in wanting judgements.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Wanting ratings correlated with activation in ventromedial prefrontal cortex (VMPFC).
source: Wanting ratings (independently of the required judgement type) correlated with activation in ventromedial prefrontal cortex (VMPFC; z = 7.32, whole-brain FWE-corrected, p < 0.001, peak = [0 44–7])
evidence: This is a neuroimaging result from the study's fMRI data analysis, also shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Wanting ratings correlated with activation in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC).
source: dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC; z = 6.63, whole-brain FWE-corrected, p < 0.001, peak = [–21 38 44])
evidence: This is a neuroimaging result from the study's fMRI data analysis, also shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Wanting ratings correlated with activation in posterior cingulate cortex (PCC).
source: and posterior cingulate cortex (PCC; z = 5.29, whole-brain FWE-corrected, p = 0.002, peak = [–3 –37 38])
evidence: This is a neuroimaging result from the study's fMRI data analysis, also shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Liking ratings correlated with BOLD signal changes in more posterior parts of PCC.
source: Liking ratings correlated with BOLD signal changes in more posterior parts of PCC (z = 4.37, whole-brain FWE-corrected, p = 0.02, peak = [–9 –64 38])
evidence: This is a neuroimaging result from the study's fMRI data analysis, also shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Liking ratings correlate with activity in orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) when applying small-volume correction.
source: Moreover, we also replicated our previous finding that liking ratings correlate with activity in orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) when applying small-volume correction (SVC; anatomical mask for the OFC based on the wfupickatlas; z = 3.20, small-volume FWE-corrected, p = 0.046, peak = [–21 50–4]).
evidence: This is a neuroimaging result from the study's fMRI data analysis, also shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The data replicate previous findings that wanting and liking are correlated with activation in VMPFC and OFC, respectively.
source: Together, these data replicate our previous findings that wanting and liking are correlated with activation in VMPFC and OFC, respectively.
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research findings.

claim: No significant effects of naltrexone or amisulpride (relative to placebo) on neural representations of wanting or liking were observed in VMPFC or OFC regions.
source: However, we observed no significant effects of naltrexone or amisulpride (relative to placebo) on these neural representations of wanting or liking in these regions (or at the whole-brain level), even at lenient statistical thresholds (p < 0.001 uncorrected, cluster size >20 voxels).
evidence: This is a null result from the study's fMRI data analysis.

claim: Wanting ratings significantly correlated with activation in the striatum during wanting judgements.
source: Consistent with our previous finding, striatal activation was significantly correlated with wanting ratings when those were behaviorally relevant (wanting ratings on wanting trials in GLM-2), z = 4.46, p = 0.003, peak = [–6 11 –1], small-volume FWE-corrected with anatomical mask for the striatum
evidence: This is a neuroimaging result from the study's fMRI data analysis, also shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Wanting-related striatal activation did not survive FWE correction at the whole-brain peak level.
source: We note that wanting-related striatal activation did not survive FWE correction at the whole-brain peak level (p = 0.14, although it did survive whole-brain FWE correction at the cluster level, p < 0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's fMRI data analysis.

claim: The wanting-related striatal activation effect appears to be somewhat weaker than in a previous study.
source: such that this effect appears to be somewhat weaker than in our previous study (Weber et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research.

claim: On wanting trials, enhanced functional coupling between striatum and DLPFC was observed as a function of increasing wanting ratings.
source: On wanting trials, we observed enhanced functional coupling between striatum and DLPFC as a function of increasing wanting ratings (wanting ratings on wanting trials: z = 3.87, small-volume FWE-corrected, p = 0.02, peak = [–21 41 41])
evidence: This is a connectivity result from the study's PPI analysis, also shown in Figure 3A.

claim: DLPFC-striatum connectivity on wanting trials was stronger for wanting than for liking ratings.
source: Moreover, DLPFC-striatum connectivity on wanting trials was stronger for wanting than for liking ratings (wanting > liking ratings on wanting trials: z = 3.64, small-volume FWE-corrected, p = 0.04, peak = [–21 41 41])
evidence: This is a connectivity result from the study's PPI analysis, also shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The wanting-dependent DLPFC-striatum coupling is consistent with previous findings that connectivity between the striatum and prefrontal correlates of wanting depends on whether wanting judgements are behaviorally relevant.
source: The wanting-dependent DLPFC-striatum coupling is consistent with previous findings that connectivity between the stratum and prefrontal correlates of wanting depends on whether wanting judgements are behaviorally relevant (Weber et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research findings.

claim: Compared with placebo, naltrexone increased DLPFC-striatum coupling for wanting relative to liking ratings on wanting trials.
source: Compared with placebo, naltrexone increased DLPFC-striatum coupling for wanting relative to liking ratings on wanting trials (naltrexone > placebo for wanting > liking ratings on wanting trials: z = 3.81, small-volume FWE-corrected, p = 0.02, peak = [–18 35 38])
evidence: This is a connectivity result from the study's PPI analysis, also shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The impact of naltrexone on DLPFC-striatum connectivity was significantly stronger on wanting than on liking trials.
source: Moreover, the impact of naltrexone on DLPFC-striatum connectivity was significantly stronger on wanting than on liking trials, ((wanting > liking ratings)wanting trials > (wanting > liking ratings)liking trials-related connectivity in the naltrexone relative to the placebo group: z = 3.55, small-volume FWE-corrected, p = 0.05, peak = [–18 35 38]).
evidence: This is a connectivity result from the study's PPI analysis.

claim: The effects of naltrexone on frontostriatal connectivity were specific for wanting judgements.
source: Thus, the effects of naltrexone on frontostriatal connectivity were specific for wanting judgements.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the connectivity analysis.

claim: No regions showed significantly reduced wanting-related connectivity under naltrexone relative to placebo.
source: We observed no further regions showing significantly reduced wanting-related connectivity under naltrexone relative to placebo
evidence: This is a null result from the study's connectivity analysis.

claim: No significant differences between amisulpride and placebo were observed in connectivity analysis.
source: and we also observed no significant differences between amisulpride and placebo as well as naltrexone and amisulpride.
evidence: This is a null result from the study's connectivity analysis.

claim: Reducing opioid neurotransmission strengthened the functional connection between the striatum and prefrontal cortex when wanting judgements were behaviorally relevant.
source: Thus, reducing opioid neurotransmission strengthened the functional connection between the striatum and prefrontal cortex when wanting judgements were behaviorally relevant.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the connectivity analysis.

claim: The test of the significance of the indirect path showed no significant mediation effect.
source: However, the test of the significance of the indirect path (which is the decisive criterion for the presence of a mediation effect; Zhao et al., 2010) showed no significant effect, ACME = –0.18, p = 0.06.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the mediation analysis.

claim: The data do not provide sufficient evidence that naltrexone effects on behavior can be explained with modulation of frontostriatal connectivity.
source: Thus, the data do not provide sufficient evidence that naltrexone effects on behavior can be explained with modulation of frontostriatal connectivity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the mediation analysis.

claim: The main effect of naltrexone on wanting ratings remained significant when controlling for DLPFC-striatum connectivity.
source: We also note that the main effect of naltrexone on wanting ratings remained significant when controlling for DLPFC-striatum connectivity, β = –8.48, t(76) = 2.54, p = 0.01
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's analysis.

claim: DLPFC-striatum connectivity was stronger for more highly wanted items in the placebo group.
source: while DLPFC-striatum connectivity was stronger for more highly wanted items in the placebo group, β = 586, t(73) = 2.30, p = 0.02.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's analysis.

claim: On liking trials, connectivity with the striatum was stronger for liking than for wanting ratings in OFC.
source: On liking trials, connectivity with the striatum was stronger for liking than for wanting ratings in OFC, (z = 3.16, small-volume FWE-corrected, p = 0.05, peak = [–33 50–7]), replicating our previous findings.
evidence: This is a connectivity result from the study's PPI analysis.

claim: No brain regions showed significant effects of naltrexone or amisulpride (relative to placebo) on liking-related connectivity with the striatum even at low, exploratory statistical thresholds.
source: However, no brain regions showed significant effects of naltrexone or amisulpride (relative to placebo) on liking-related connectivity with the striatum even at low, exploratory statistical thresholds (p < 0.001, cluster size >20 voxels).
evidence: This is a null result from the study's connectivity analysis.

claim: The significant Naltrexone × Judgement × Relevance interaction replicated the finding that naltrexone had dissociable effects on wanting and liking as a function of the behavioral relevance of these reward components.
source: The significant Naltrexone× Judgement × Relevance interaction, β = 6.0e-03, t(452) = 2.46, p = 0.01, replicated the finding that naltrexone had dissociable effects on wanting and liking as a function of the behavioral relevance of these reward components.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ROI analysis.

claim: A significant Amisulpride × Relevance interaction was observed.
source: We also observed a significant Amisulpride × Relevance interaction, β = 4.1e-03, t(452) = 2.42, p = 0.02.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ROI analysis.

claim: In wanting trials, DLPFC-striatum connectivity was enhanced for wanting compared with liking ratings under naltrexone.
source: Separate analyses for wanting and liking judgements revealed that in wanting trials DLPFC-striatum connectivity was enhanced for wanting compared with liking ratings under both naltrexone, Naltrexone× Relevance interaction, β = 5.6e-03, t(226) = 3.19, p = 0.002
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ROI analysis, also shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In wanting trials, DLPFC-striatum connectivity was enhanced for wanting compared with liking ratings under amisulpride.
source: and amisulpride, Amisulpride × Relevance interaction, β = 4.1e-03, t(226) = 2.35, p = 0.02
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ROI analysis, also shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Liking judgements showed no significant effects of naltrexone or amisulpride relative to placebo.
source: In contrast, liking judgements showed no significant effects of naltrexone or amisulpride relative to placebo, all t < 1.34, all p > 0.18
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ROI analysis, also shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The current findings provide evidence for dissociable roles of opioidergic neurotransmission in processing the two dimensions of rewards on both a behavioral and a neural level.
source: The current findings provide evidence for dissociable roles of opioidergic neurotransmission in processing the two dimensions of rewards on both a behavioral and a neural level.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study's findings.

claim: Lowering opioidergic activation with naltrexone selectively reduced wanting, not liking, ratings for non-consumable goods.
source: Behaviorally, lowering opioidergic activation with naltrexone selectively reduced wanting, not liking, ratings for non-consumable goods.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral findings.

claim: The reduction in wanting under naltrexone was reflected by changes in DLPFC-striatum connectivity.
source: On a neural level, this reduction in wanting was reflected by changes in DLPFC-striatum connectivity
evidence: This is a summary of the neural findings.

claim: When wanting judgements were required, DLPFC-striatum connectivity was significantly stronger for the behaviorally relevant wanting ratings than for the irrelevant liking dimension of rewards.
source: When wanting judgements were required, DLPFC-striatum connectivity was significantly stronger for the behaviorally relevant wanting ratings than for the irrelevant liking dimension of rewards.
evidence: This is a summary of the connectivity findings.

claim: Wanting-related functional coupling between DLPFC and striatum was significantly stronger under naltrexone than under placebo.
source: Importantly, wanting-related functional coupling between DLPFC and striatum was significantly stronger under naltrexone than under placebo.
evidence: This is a summary of the drug effect on connectivity.

claim: This finding is consistent with recent findings relating opioid receptor inhibition with increased connectivity between the prefrontal control system and reward circuits.
source: This is consistent with recent findings relating opioid receptor inhibition with increased connectivity between the prefrontal control system and reward circuits (Elton et al., 2019; Lim et al., 2019)

claim: Prefrontal kappa opioid receptors mediate the impact of naltrexone on drug craving in alcohol use disorder.
source: and suggesting prefrontal kappa opioid receptors to mediate the impact of naltrexone on drug craving in alcohol use disorder (de Laat et al., 2019).

claim: Through corticostriatal loops, the striatum receives input from several cortical regions and can prioritize processing of behaviorally relevant information.
source: Through corticostriatal loops, the striatum receives input from several cortical regions and can prioritize processing of behaviorally relevant information (Frank, 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about brain function supported by citation.

claim: DLPFC provides inhibitory input to the striatum and was shown to reduce wanting-related activation in the striatum.
source: DLPFC provides inhibitory input to the striatum and was shown to reduce wanting-related activation in the striatum (Dong et al., 2020; Koob and Volkow, 2010)

claim: Frontostriatal loops are important for self-control.
source: consistent with the importance of frontostriatal loops for self-control (van den Bos et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about brain function supported by citation.

claim: The observed positive relationship between wanting ratings and DLPFC-striatum connectivity might indicate that DLPFC exerts top-down control over striatal representations of wanting predominantly for highly wanted items.
source: According to this view, the observed positive relationship between wanting ratings and DLPFC-striatum connectivity might indicate that DLPFC exerts top-down control over striatal representations of wanting predominantly for highly wanted items, whereas there may be less need for inhibitory top-down control for less desired goods (van den Bos et al., 2014).

claim: By strengthening DLPFC-striatum connectivity, naltrexone enhances top-down processes predominantly for highly wanted items.
source: By strengthening DLPFC-striatum connectivity, naltrexone enhances top-down processes predominantly for highly wanted items, which would explain why lower wanting under naltrexone is associated with stronger DLPFC-striatum connectivity even though in the placebo group functional DLPFC-striatum coupling is increased for highly wanted items.

claim: Because no significant brain-behavior mediation effect was observed (p = 0.06), the stronger DLPFC-striatum connectivity under naltrexone should not be interpreted as the cause for the changes in behavioral ratings under naltrexone.
source: In any case, because we observed no significant brain-behavior mediation effect (p = 0.06), the stronger DLPFC-striatum connectivity under naltrexone should not be interpreted as the cause for the changes in behavioral ratings under naltrexone.

claim: In the current study, significant effects were observed predominantly in the left hemisphere.
source: It is further worth noting that in the current study we observed significant effects predominantly in the left hemisphere.

claim: In the literature on frontostriatal connectivity during reward processing, both left- and right-lateralized effects were reported.
source: In the literature on frontostriatal connectivity during reward processing, both left- and right-lateralized effects were reported (van den Bos et al., 2014; van den Bos et al., 2015; Yuan et al., 2017).

claim: The study does not make claims regarding whether the left-lateralized result pattern represents just a power issue or a truly lateralized effect.
source: We therefore do not make any claims regarding whether this result pattern represents just a power issue or a truly lateralized effect.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of interpreting the findings.

source: Contrary to our hypotheses, we did not observe effects of naltrexone on liking

claim: The study did not observe amisulpride effects on wanting.
source: or amisulpride effects on wanting.

source: Interestingly, however, a recent study observed no influences of opioid and dopamine antagonists on self-report wanting and liking ratings but only on experimental measures of these reward dimensions (Korb et al., 2020).

claim: Previous studies reporting effects of dopaminergic manipulations on wanting operationalized wanting with experimental measures rather than self-report.
source: In fact, previous studies reporting effects of dopaminergic manipulations on wanting operationalized wanting with experimental measures rather than self-report (Soutschek et al., 2020a; Soutschek et al., 2020b; Weber et al., 2016)
evidence: This is a statement about prior research methods.

claim: Studies using self-report ratings observed no or only weak effects of pharmacological manipulations.
source: while studies using self-report ratings observed no or only weak effects of pharmacological manipulations (Case et al., 2016; Ellingsen et al., 2014; Løseth et al., 2019).

claim: Implicit measures of liking such as face muscle activity are more open to alternative interpretations.

claim: The study's measurements might have been less sensitive than those of other studies assessing the liking of consumed rewards because participants had to provide liking ratings without being able to actually consume or handle the items.
source: Moreover, given that in our study participants had to provide liking ratings without being able to actually consume or handle the items, our measurements might have been less sensitive than those of other studies assessing the liking of consumed rewards (Buchel et al., 2018; Chelnokova et al., 2014; Eikemo et al., 2016).

claim: It has recently been suggested that amisulpride shows, if any, only weak effects on BOLD signal changes in the reward system.
